name: ujson (µjson)
workload: nativejson-benchmark DOM parse, stringify and prettify of canada.json (2199KB), citm_catalog.json (1737KB) and twitter.json (632KB), time summed over the three files, in memory.
claimed_speedup: Independent shootout rows, derived from page data (CSV times summed over the 3 files): parse 37.15 ms vs nlohmann 72.48 ms (1.95x faster; per file canada 25.19 vs 55.59 ms, citm 8.21 vs 9.88 ms, twitter 3.76 vs 7.01 ms); stringify 24.86 vs 87.73 ms (3.5x); prettify 29.28 vs 130.56 ms (4.5x). DOM traversal (Statistics) is slower: 3.02 vs 2.17 ms (1.4x slower). The project's own README makes only the unquantified claim 'Fast UTF-8 conformant parser'.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS; build script build/premake5.lua (release config: -DNDEBUG, premake optimize "Full", gmake buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra) read from the repo head, so the 2016 sample build is assumed to match
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80 GHz
stars_or_usage: Bitbucket repo with no star count; listed in awesome-cpp (JSON) and one of 43 libraries in miloyip/nativejson-benchmark
tradeoffs: Much higher memory than nlohmann in the same run: parse result 34.37 MB vs 5.29 MB on canada.json (6.5x), 16.23 MB vs 3.05 MB on citm_catalog.json. Four-file amalgamation (ujson.hpp, ujson.cpp, double-conversion.h, double-conversion.cc); scanner generated by re2c; C++11; objects are sorted vectors with binary-search lookup; UTF-8 only; code size 126,996 bytes vs nlohmann 42,132 bytes in the benchmark's jsonstat executable.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2016 sample run (README 'Update on 2016-9-9'), a sister project of RapidJSON's author, with the 2015-04-12 ujson version; the author's later commit of 2016-10-08 'Greatly reduce memory usage at the cost of slight reduction in parse speed' postdates it. Baseline nlohmann/json is v2.0.3, many releases behind the current library. Flags are read from the benchmark's current premake5.lua, not from the 2016 run. Conformance in the same suite: parse validation 33/34 (fails pass01), parse double 66/66, parse string 9/9, roundtrip 18/27, against nlohmann 34/34, 66/66, 9/9, 23/27. Not compared against libstdc++, libc++ or MSVC STL (no std JSON exists). Project has no benchmark of its own.

name: UltraJSON
workload: Python loads/dumps of the twitter.json, github.json, citm_catalog.json and canada.json fixtures, median latency per call, measured in the orjson project's README (Python 3.10.5, ujson 5.4.0).
claimed_speedup: orjson 3.9.4 README (an independent competitor's benchmark), median latency ujson vs json, derived ratios from page data: canada.json serialize 14.16 vs 35.7 ms (2.5x faster), deserialize 8.73 vs 21.1 ms (2.4x); citm_catalog.json serialize 2.89 vs 3.93 ms (1.4x), deserialize 3.5 vs 4.99 ms (1.4x); twitter.json serialize 1.68 vs 1.8 ms (1.07x), deserialize 1.87 vs 2.45 ms (1.3x); github.json serialize 0.18 vs 0.18 ms (tie), deserialize 0.19 vs 0.16 ms (ujson slower).
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.10.5 on Linux (amd64) with ujson 5.4.0 per the orjson README; the ujson wheel's compiler and flags are not stated. The project's own README lists CPython 3.11.3 built with GCC 11.3.0.
hardware: Linux amd64, CPU model not stated in the orjson README; the project's own README gives only 'Linux 5.15.0-1037-azure x86_64'.
stars_or_usage: 4.5k stars; widely installed Python package (ujson on PyPI)
tradeoffs: Project is in maintenance-only mode: its README warns that 'UltraJSON's architecture is fundamentally ill-suited to making changes without risk of introducing new security vulnerabilities' (buffer overflows) and recommends migrating to orjson, which it calls much faster. Defaults differ from json.dumps (ensure_ascii=True, escape_forward_slashes=True), so output is not byte-identical without options. The orjson 3.9.4 README reports that ujson 5.4.0 segfaulted in its int-keys sort benchmark and that ujson.loads of a lone surrogate escape returns an empty string instead of raising.
caveats: Baseline is Python's stdlib json, not a C++ library, and the guessed baseline list (nlohmann/json) does not apply. The advantage is workload-dependent and small on modern CPython: tie on github.json serialize, slower on github.json deserialize. The orjson benchmark is run by a rival library's author, with no CPU model or flags, hence tier B. First-party numbers in https://github.com/ultrajson/ultrajson README (calls/s, higher better; ujson 5.7.1.dev26 vs json 2.0.9, CPython 3.11.3, benchmark script tests/benchmark.py in the repo): medium complex object encode 11,672 vs 5,729 (2.0x), decode 12,522 vs 9,720 (1.3x); array of 256 doubles encode 18,282 vs 5,935 (3.1x), decode 28,765 vs 13,367 (2.2x); but array of 256 strings decode 28,518 vs 42,221 and array of 256 UTF-8 strings encode 3,457 vs 3,653 are slower than json. The same README shows ujson far behind orjson (e.g. 256 doubles encode 18,282 vs 79,569). The C decoder core wrapped by the archived esnme/ujson4c also appears in nativejson-benchmark (parse of 3 files 8.95 ms vs nlohmann 72.48 ms) but fails 32 of 66 parse-double and 4 of 9 parse-string conformance tests there.

name: xlsx_drone
baseline: roo (Ruby gem Roo::Excelx), fastest of four Ruby xlsx readers in the benchmark
workload: Ruby binding (xlsx_drone_rb) reading every cell of a 200,000 row x 3 column xlsx (number, string, date) with the C library, against roo, creek, rubyXL and simple_xlsx_reader.
claimed_speedup: README: 'x2 times faster than the fastest one'. Screenshot of 'rake bm' (real seconds): xlsx_drone 10.63, roo 20.41, simple_xlsx_reader 25.49, creek 28.27, rubyXL 79.56; xlsx_drone is 1.9x faster than roo, 2.4x than simple_xlsx_reader, 2.7x than creek and 7.5x than rubyXL (derived from page data).
hardware: 'my old notebook' per the README; CPU model, OS version, Ruby version and C build flags not stated
tradeoffs: Read-only (writing is on hold); focus 'speed over functionality'; copy src and ext folders into the project; depends on bundled kuba--/zip 0.3.2 and sxmlc 4.5.4 (BSD-style); cells are looked up by row and column letters; the last column is not computed on load because it costs time on big files. Open issues include an incompatibility with Apache POI generated files (#14) and a crash on an odd format (#12, closed).
caveats: The benchmark lives in the Ruby binding repo and measures the C library through Ruby FFI, not the C API itself; baselines are other Ruby gems, not openpyxl or a C reader such as xlsxio. Result is a screenshot from the author's own machine with the benchmark script test/benchmark/speed.rb and a 200,000-row file in the repo, but no CPU, flags or Ruby version, so tier C. Readers do different work: the benchmark script's own comment says simple_xlsx_reader cannot tell numbers from strings, and each library builds a different in-memory structure. No numeric comparison in the C repo README, CHANGELOG or issues. Category binary-schemas is a loose fit (spreadsheet file reader over zip and XML).

name: YAJL
baseline: json-c 0.12.1 (also JsonCpp 1.0.0 and Jansson v2.7 in the same suite)
workload: nativejson-benchmark DOM parse (yajl_tree_parse) of canada.json (2199KB), citm_catalog.json (1737KB) and twitter.json (632KB), time summed over the three files, plus DOM traversal (Statistics).
claimed_speedup: Project README: 'YAJL is fast ... My hope is that YAJL will perform comparably to the fastest JSON parser out there' (no numbers). Independent shootout rows, derived from page data: DOM parse 103.45 ms vs json-c 134.55 ms (1.30x faster), JsonCpp 165.52 ms (1.60x), Jansson 112.06 ms (1.08x); per file canada 75.62 vs 105.78 ms (json-c), citm 19.55 vs 21.12 ms, twitter 8.28 vs 7.65 ms (YAJL slower). DOM traversal (Statistics) 1.07 ms vs json-c 2.99, JsonCpp 2.62, Jansson 1.62.
compiler_and_flags: clang 7.0 64-bit on macOS; build script build/premake5.lua (release config: -DNDEBUG, premake optimize "Full", gmake buildoptions -march=native -Wall -Wextra) read from the repo head, so the 2016 sample build is assumed to match
hardware: MacBook Pro (Retina, 15-inch, Mid 2015), Core i7-4980HQ @ 2.80 GHz
tradeoffs: Streaming SAX-style callbacks, incremental parsing off a stream, tiny and portable ANSI C, verbose error messages; the tree API used in the benchmark (yajl_tree_parse) is a convenience layer. In the benchmark's canada.json parse the DOM uses 12.9 MB vs json-c 33.7 MB, but needs 501,567 allocations vs 390,651.
caveats: Mixed result, YAJL is mid-pack: DOM parse ranks 24th of 40 libraries; it is slower than nlohmann v2.0.3 (72.48 ms), cJSON (24.67 ms), ujson4c, RapidJSON (7.93 ms, 13x faster), and slower than json-c on stringify (78.64 vs 30.80 ms) and prettify (102.12 vs 49.26 ms). SAX round-trip 124.52 ms vs RapidJSON 18.14 ms and SAX statistics 47.35 vs 6.32 ms, so the README's 'comparable to the fastest parser' is not supported. Conformance in the same suite: parse validation 34/34, parse double 57/66, parse string 8/9, roundtrip 21/27. The sample is a 2016 macOS run by a RapidJSON author; flags are read from the benchmark's current premake5.lua. The project's ChangeLog mentions an in-tree perf/perftest.c benchmark and its TODO file lists 'some performance comparison against json_checker'; no comparison numbers were found in either.
